mainTopic: Two-story houses: dividing the materials when a house owned by two people collapses, and the rights of an upstairs renter whose floor breaks.
overview: The amud opens with a משנה about a two-story house owned by two people that collapses. The owners split the fallen materials, the court looks at which stones were likely to break, and a man who recognizes his own stones takes them as part of his share. The גמרא first narrows the even split to cases where nobody can know how the house fell or whose stones they are. It then explains that the partner who recognizes his stones wins only because the other partner says 'I don't know.' The גמרא shows this fits רב נחמן, because the case involves an oath that partner cannot take. רבא and אביי then argue over whether the recognized stones count against the broken stones or the whole ones. A second משנה rules that a renter whose upper story breaks may live downstairs until the owner repairs it, and רבי יוסי adds how two owners share the cost of the ceiling. The גמרא discusses how big the break must be, where רב and שמואל disagree, and what wording of the rental gives the renter a claim on the house below. רב אשי's answer is backed by a case about a vine sold 'on top of this peach tree.' The amud ends as רבי אבא בר ממל begins a new question.

steps.title: The משנה: Dividing a Collapsed Two-Story House
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that the two owners split the fallen materials. The court considers which stones were likely to break, and recognized stones go to their owner and count toward his share.
steps.simpleTranslation: If a house and the upper story above it belong to two different people and they collapse, both owners split the wood, the stones and the earth. The court looks at which stones were likely to break. If one of them recognizes some of his own stones, he takes them, and they are counted as part of his share.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה sets out three rules for a collapsed two-story house owned by two people. The materials are split, the court looks at which stones likely broke, and a man who recognizes his own stones takes them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One person owns the bottom floor (הבית) and another owns the floor above it (העלייה), so when it all falls nobody knows whose stones are whose. The basic rule is to split. The court still tries to work out whose stones broke, so that the broken ones go to their likely owner. Recognized stones are not a bonus; they count toward that person's half.

keyTerms.meaning: The ground-floor house and the upper story built on top of it

steps.confusionAlert: Recognizing your stones does not give you extra. You take those stones, but they are subtracted from your half, and the other owner gets that much more from the rest.

phrases.aramaic: מַתְנִי׳ הַבַּיִת וְהָעֲלִיָּיה שֶׁל שְׁנַיִם, שֶׁנָּפְלוּ –
phrases.english: MISHNA: The house and the upper story belonging to two people, that collapsed —
phrases.notes: One person owns the bottom floor and a different person owns the floor built on top of it.

phrases.english: the two of them divide
the timber, the stones and the earth.
And the court considers which stones
were likely to break.
If one of them
recognized some of his stones —
he takes them, and they count toward his amount.

steps.mimraCoreRuling: The owners split the fallen materials. The court considers which stones likely broke, and recognized stones go to their owner as part of his share.

steps.title: Inference: The Court Can Sometimes Tell How It Fell
steps.stepSummary: From the word רואין, the גמרא concludes that the court can sometimes tell whether the house fell by collapsing from below or by crashing down from above.
steps.simpleTranslation: Since the משנה says 'the court considers,' we learn that it is possible to figure out from the stones how the building fell: whether it sank from below, or whether it fell with a crash from above.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא reads closely into the משנה's word רואין. That word shows the court can work out how the collapse happened.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two ways a two-story house can fall. In חבסא the bottom gives way and the top sinks down, so the bottom stones get crushed. In חבטא the top crashes down, so the top stones break. If the court can tell which happened, it knows whose stones broke.

keyTerms.meaning: From the fact that the משנה teaches
To establish the facts about them
Falling by pressure: the lower story caves in and the top sinks down
Falling with a blow: the upper story crashes down

steps.confusionAlert: חבסא and חבטא sound almost the same. חבסא is pressure from sinking, which crushes the lower stones. חבטא is a blow from the top falling, which breaks the upper stones.

phrases.english: GEMARA: From the fact that the mishna teaches 'considers' —
it can be inferred that it is possible to establish the facts about them,
phrases.notes: 'Them' means the stones: looking at the rubble can show what happened.

phrases.english: whether it fell with pressure,
or whether it fell with a blow.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִדְּקָתָנֵי רוֹאִין מִכְּלָל דְּאִיכָּא לְמֵיקַם עֲלַיְיהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Reads a single word of the משנה closely to learn the facts of its case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The משנה assumes the manner of the collapse can sometimes be determined from the stones.

steps.title: Challenge: Why Split Evenly in the First Clause?
steps.stepSummary: If the manner of collapse can be known, why does the first part of the משנה split everything evenly? The court should check how the house fell and award the unbroken stones to the right person.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, why do they split in the first part? Let us look. If it fell with a blow, the upper stones broke. If it fell with pressure, the lower stones broke.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא uses the inference it just made to challenge the first ruling of the משנה, the simple even split.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the court can tell how the house fell, then it knows whose stones broke. The broken stones belong to one owner, and the whole stones belong to the other. So why does the רישא (first clause) just divide everything without checking?

keyTerms.meaning: The first clause of the משנה
The upper stones / the lower stones

phrases.english: If so, why in the first clause do they divide?
Let us see: if it fell with a blow —
the upper ones broke,
if it fell with pressure —
the lower ones broke!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns the inference from step 2 against the even split in step 1.
steps.kashyaTarget: The even-split ruling in the first clause of the משנה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the stones show how the house fell, the court should use that to decide ownership instead of splitting evenly.

steps.title: Answer: The House Fell at Night
steps.stepSummary: The first clause is talking about a house that fell at night, when nobody saw how it came down.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is needed for a case where it fell at night.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by limiting the first clause to a case where the house fell at night.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The even split applies only when nobody saw the collapse happen. The later clause, רואין, applies when the facts can be found out.

keyTerms.meaning: It is needed only for this case

phrases.english: No, it is necessary where it fell at night.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 3.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The first clause seemed to apply even when the manner of collapse could be known.
steps.terutzMaskana: The first clause applies when nobody witnessed the collapse.

steps.title: Challenge: Look at the Stones in the Morning
steps.stepSummary: Even if the house fell at night, people could look at the rubble the next morning.
steps.simpleTranslation: But let them look at them in the morning!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the night answer: the stones are still lying there in the morning.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 2 said the stones themselves show how the house fell. So not seeing the collapse should not matter, since the evidence is still there to check by daylight.

phrases.english: But let them see them in the morning?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer given in step 4.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that the house fell at night
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The rubble still shows how the house fell, so nighttime alone does not leave the facts unknown.

steps.title: Answer: The Stones Were Cleared Away
steps.stepSummary: The rubble was cleared away before morning, so there was nothing left to look at.
steps.simpleTranslation: Where they cleared them away.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds another detail to the case: the stones were removed before anyone could study them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once the stones have been moved, you can no longer see how they landed. The evidence is gone, so the facts cannot be determined.

phrases.english: Where they cleared them away.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 5.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The rubble could be looked at in the morning.
steps.terutzMaskana: The rubble had already been cleared, so it could not be examined.

steps.title: Challenge: Ask Whoever Cleared the Stones
steps.stepSummary: Then find out who cleared the stones and ask them how the rubble looked.
steps.simpleTranslation: But let them see who cleared them away, and ask him!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges again: the people who moved the stones saw the rubble and could tell what happened.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Whoever cleared the stones saw how they were lying. Their testimony would answer the question, so the court still would not need to split evenly.

phrases.english: But let them see who cleared them away and ask him?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer given in step 6.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that the stones were cleared away
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The people who cleared the stones are witnesses who could report what they saw.

steps.title: Answer: Passersby Cleared Them and Left
steps.stepSummary: Random people from the public street cleared the stones and went on their way, so nobody can be found to ask.
steps.simpleTranslation: Where people of the public domain cleared them away and went off into the world.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes defining the case: the stones were cleared by strangers who cannot be traced.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now every way of learning how the house fell has been closed off. Nobody saw the fall, the rubble is gone, and the people who cleared it cannot be located. The next step asks whether the place where the stones are lying could still decide who owns them.

keyTerms.meaning: People of the public domain; random passersby
They went off into the world, gone and untraceable

steps.whatToRemember: The משנה's even split applies only when there is no way to know how the house fell: it fell at night, the stones were cleared, and the strangers who cleared them are gone. When the manner of collapse can be known, the court looks at it (רואין) and assigns the broken stones to their likely owner.

phrases.english: Where people of the public domain cleared them away,
and went off into the world.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּפַנִּינְהוּ בְּנֵי רְשׁוּת הָרַבִּים וַאֲזַלוּ לְעָלְמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 7 and completes the definition of the first clause's case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The people who cleared the stones could be asked.
steps.terutzMaskana: The stones were cleared by strangers who cannot be found, so the facts can never be known and the owners split evenly.

steps.title: Check whose property the stones are lying on
steps.stepSummary: Even with no witnesses, the location of the stones should show who owns them. Whoever wants stones lying on the other's land must bring proof.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let them see in whose property the stones are lying, and the other one should be treated as someone taking from his friend, who must bring proof!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises another challenge. Even if nobody saw how the house fell or how the rubble looked, we can still see where the stones are lying now.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Steps 5-8 closed off every way to learn how the walls fell. Now the גמרא uses a different tool: whoever's property the stones sit on counts as holding them. So the other partner is המוציא מחבירו and needs proof, which means the stones should not simply be split.

keyTerms.meaning: Let them see, let them check
Whoever wants to take from his friend must bring proof

phrases.english: But let them see in whose property they are lying
phrases.notes: 'They' means the fallen stones. Some versions add the letter in square brackets, but the meaning stays the same.

phrases.english: and let the other one be
one who takes from his friend, who must bring proof!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After step 8 ruled out finding out how the rubble looked, this step suggests using where the stones are lying instead.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's ruling that the stones are split when nobody knows whose they are
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Location is a form of possession. The partner whose land holds the stones should keep them unless the other brings proof.

steps.title: The stones are in a shared courtyard or the street
steps.stepSummary: The משנה is talking about stones lying in a courtyard both partners own, or in the public street, so neither partner holds them.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, the case is needed where the stones are lying in a courtyard that belongs to both of them, or else in the public street.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by narrowing the case. The stones landed somewhere that does not belong to just one partner.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Location only helps when the place belongs to one side. In a shared courtyard or in רשות הרבים, neither partner has possession, so neither one is המוציא. That is why splitting still makes sense.

keyTerms.meaning: No, it is needed for this case (the ruling is about a specific situation)
A courtyard belonging to both of them

phrases.english: No, it is needed
where they are lying in a courtyard of both of them
or else, in the public street

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 9 by placing the stones where nobody has sole possession.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The stones are lying on one partner's land, so location decides.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה is about stones in a shared or public place, so location proves nothing.

steps.title: Partners don't mind each other's things on their side
steps.stepSummary: A second answer: even if the stones are on one partner's side, partners like these don't care if each other's belongings sit there, so location proves nothing.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you want, say: partners in a situation like this are not strict with each other.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives another answer to the same challenge. This time it keeps the stones on one partner's land.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Land normally 'holds' what is on it because owners don't let other people's things sit there. Partners, however, let each other leave things around, so the stones lying on one side do not show they belong to him.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you want, say (a second answer)
They are not strict, they don't mind

phrases.english: And if you want, say
partners in a situation like this
are not strict with each other

steps.whatToRemember: The משנה splits the stones because nothing tells us whose they are. Witnesses, the rubble, the people who cleared it, and the place they lie are all ruled out.
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second answer to step 9 that does not need to change the location of the stones.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Removing the basis of the proof
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Stones lying on someone's side show they belong to him.
steps.terutzMaskana: Between partners, where something lies proves nothing.

steps.title: What is the other partner saying?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the next line of the משנה, where one partner recognizes his stones, and asks what the other partner claims.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'If one of them recognized,' etc. And the other one, what does he claim? If he says yes, it's obvious! And if he doesn't say yes, why does the first one take them?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new line in the משנה. It asks how the other partner responds when one partner says, 'These stones are mine.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each simple option fails. If the other agrees, the משנה would be telling us something obvious. If he argues back, there is no reason to believe the first partner. So there must be a third possibility.

phrases.aramaic: אִם הָיָה אֶחָד מֵהֶן מַכִּיר כּוּ׳
phrases.english: If one of them recognized, etc.
phrases.notes: This is a quote from the משנה. It goes on to say he takes the stones he recognizes.

phrases.english: And the other one, what does he claim?
If he says yes, it's obvious!
And if he does not say yes,
why does he take them?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic: the next line of the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the other partner answers when one partner claims to recognize his stones

steps.title: He says 'I don't know'
steps.stepSummary: The other partner says he doesn't know whose stones they are, so the partner who makes a clear claim takes them.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, the case is where he says to him: I don't know.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the only option left. The other partner neither agrees nor argues; he just says he doesn't know.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the middle option between 'yes' and 'no.' It is not obvious, and it explains why the one who says 'I'm sure' wins. A sure claim beats an 'I don't know.' This sets up the next step.

phrases.english: Rather, where he says to him: I don't know

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 12.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The other partner says 'I don't know,' and the partner who is sure takes the stones.

steps.title: Does this disprove רב נחמן?
steps.stepSummary: The משנה seems to say that 'I don't know' loses to a sure claim. That would go against רב נחמן, who holds that someone sued for a מנה who says 'I don't know' is פטור.
steps.simpleTranslation: Shall we say this is a refutation of רב נחמן? For it was stated: 'I have a מנה in your hand,' and the other says, 'I don't know.' רב הונא and רב יהודה say he is liable. רב נחמן and רבי יוחנן say he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא uses step 13 to challenge רב נחמן. It brings a known argument about someone who answers a claim with 'I don't know.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the argument, רב נחמן says a sure claim against an 'I don't know' answer does not force payment. Our משנה, as explained in step 13, gives the stones to the one who is sure. So the משנה seems to side with רב הונא and רב יהודה.

keyTerms.meaning: A sure claim against an 'I don't know' (the name of this topic)

steps.confusionAlert: Here רב נחמן is the one who says 'פטור.' Don't mix up the sides: רב הונא and רב יהודה make the 'I don't know' person pay, and רב נחמן and רבי יוחנן do not.

phrases.english: Shall we say this is a refutation of Rav Nachman
for it was stated:
'I have a maneh in your hand'
phrases.notes: He means: you owe me a מנה, which is a hundred דינרים.

phrases.english: and the other says: 'I don't know'

phrases.aramaic: רַב הוּנָא וְרַב יְהוּדָה אָמְרִי: חַיָּיב
phrases.english: Rav Huna and Rav Yehuda say: he is liable

phrases.aramaic: רַב נַחְמָן וְרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן אָמְרִי: פָּטוּר.
phrases.english: Rav Nachman and Rabbi Yochanan say: he is exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the explanation from step 13 to challenge רב נחמן.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב נחמן's ruling that the 'I don't know' person is פטור
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה lets a sure claim beat 'I don't know,' which goes against רב נחמן's ruling.

steps.title: The משנה is a case where he already owes a שבועה
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן himself agrees that 'I don't know' loses when there is already a שבועה between the two sides. The משנה is that kind of case.
steps.simpleTranslation: As רב נחמן says, for example where there is a matter of a שבועה between them. Here too, it is a case where there is a matter of a שבועה between them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רב נחמן. It uses רב נחמן's own exception and says the משנה falls into that exception.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב נחמן agrees the 'I don't know' person must pay when he already owes a שבועה he cannot swear, because he doesn't know. The גמרא says the משנה is also a case like that. So the משנה fits רב נחמן and is no proof against him.

keyTerms.meaning: A matter of an oath (an oath he already owes)

steps.whatToRemember: The 'I don't know' partner loses in the משנה only because he already owes a שבועה he cannot take. That fits רב נחמן's own exception, so the משנה does not disprove him.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that the rule of a sure claim against 'I don't know' depends on whether a שבועה is already owed. That idea comes back in many money cases.

phrases.english: As Rav Nachman says
for example, where there is a matter of an oath between them
phrases.notes: רב נחמן agrees the 'I don't know' person pays here, because he owes an oath he can't swear.

phrases.english: Here too
it is where there is a matter of an oath between them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 14 by placing the משנה inside רב נחמן's own exception.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case using the disputant's own exception
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה shows that a sure claim always beats 'I don't know,' against רב נחמן.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה is a case with a שבועה already owed, where רב נחמן also agrees the 'I don't know' person loses.

steps.title: What counts as a 'matter of an oath'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for an example of the kind of case רב נחמן agrees to, where an oath is already involved.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is a case of 'a matter of an oath'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for a concrete example of the 'matter of an oath' it mentioned in the last step. This sets up the next step, where it gives רבא's case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 15 the גמרא said רב נחמן agrees that 'I don't know' loses when a שבועה is already involved. Now it wants to know what that kind of case looks like in practice.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case? How does it look?
A situation where an oath is already involved between the two sides

phrases.english: What is the case of 'a matter of an oath'?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for an example of the term used in the answer of step 15
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A clear example of a case where a שבועה is already involved, so that 'I don't know' loses

steps.title: רבא's case: admits fifty, doesn't know about the rest
steps.stepSummary: Someone is claimed a מנה. He admits fifty and says he doesn't know about the rest. He must swear but can't, so he pays.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is like רבא's case. רבא said: One says, 'You have a מנה of mine.' The other says, 'You only have fifty with me, and about the rest I don't know.' Since he cannot swear, he must pay.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with רבא's case. A man who admits part of the claim would normally have to swear about the rest, but since he says 'I don't know,' he can't swear, so he has to pay.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Admitting part of a claim brings a שבועה from the תורה on the rest. Saying 'I don't know' makes it impossible to swear honestly. Because the oath is already required and he can't take it, he loses, so this is the kind of case where even רב נחמן agrees.

keyTerms.meaning: A sum of one hundred זוז
And about the rest, I don't know
Since he cannot swear, he pays

steps.whatToRemember: A 'matter of an oath' means he already owes a שבועה. If he says 'I don't know,' he can't swear, so he pays.
steps.whyThisMatters: This rule, 'since he cannot swear, he pays,' is a well-known principle in דיני ממונות and explains why 'I don't know' can lose even according to רב נחמן.

phrases.english: Like the case of רבא.
As רבא said:
"I have a מנה in your hand,"
and the other one says:
"You have only fifty in my hand,"
phrases.notes: By admitting part of the claim, he now owes a שבועה on the other fifty.

phrases.english: "and about the rest, I don't know."
Since he cannot swear,
he must pay.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 16
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A case like רבא's: partial admission plus 'I don't know' about the rest. He owes an oath he can't take, so he pays.

steps.title: רבא's first reading: the stones count against the broken ones
steps.stepSummary: On the משנה's line 'they count toward his amount,' רבא first thought the recognized whole stones are counted against the broken stones, which shows the 'I don't know' partner is weaker.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says: 'And they count toward his amount.' רבא thought to say this means toward the count of broken stones. This shows that since the other partner said 'I don't know,' he is worse off.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the next line of the משנה and gives רבא's first understanding of it. רבא reads it so that the partner who recognized his stones comes out ahead.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The partner takes the whole stones he recognizes, and רבא says these are counted as if he took broken stones. So the other partner only gets broken stones to match, and the recognizer ends up with more whole stones. רבא learns from this that the one who said 'I don't know' is in the weaker position.

keyTerms.meaning: And they count toward his amount (his share)
He thought to say (a first idea that may be dropped later)
Is worse off; has a weaker position

phrases.english: "And they count toward his amount."
phrases.notes: This is the next line of the משנה: the stones he recognized are counted as part of his share.

phrases.english: רבא thought to say
that it is according to the count of broken stones.
This shows that since he said "I don't know,"
he is worse off.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to the next line of the משנה after finishing the oath discussion
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Recognized whole stones count against the broken stones, because the 'I don't know' partner is weaker

steps.title: אביי: the partner who recognized stones is the weaker one
steps.stepSummary: אביי argues the opposite: since the partner only recognizes these stones, he can claim nothing more, and all the rest belong to the other partner.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to him: On the contrary, this one is worse off. Since he knows these, he doesn't know about any more, so he has nothing further, and all the others belong to the other partner!
steps.whatsHappening: אביי rejects רבא's reading. He says the partner who recognized some stones is the one in the weaker position.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By saying 'these are mine,' the recognizer shows he knows of no other whole stones that are his. So he has no claim to extra whole stones, and the rest go to his partner. That flips רבא's logic.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two partners. 'This one' in אביי's words is the partner who DID recognize his stones, not the one who said 'I don't know.'

phrases.english: אביי said to him:
On the contrary, this one is worse off.
Since he knows these,
he doesn't know about any more,
so he has nothing further,
and all the others belong to the other one!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects רבא's reading from step 18
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: רבא's reading that the stones count against the broken ones, and his claim that the 'I don't know' partner is weaker
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The recognizer only knows these stones are his, so he has no claim to any more whole stones

steps.title: אביי's reading: the stones count against the whole ones
steps.stepSummary: אביי explains the משנה to mean the recognized stones are counted against the whole stones.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, אביי said: It is according to the count of whole stones.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי gives his own reading of the משנה in place of רבא's.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The recognized whole stones count as part of his share of whole stones. The other partner then takes a matching number of whole stones, so neither one gets extra whole stones.

phrases.english: Rather, אביי said:
It is according to the count of whole stones.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a new reading after rejecting רבא's in step 19
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The stones count against the broken ones (רבא)
steps.terutzMaskana: The stones count against the whole ones (אביי)

steps.title: Then what does recognizing his stones gain him?
steps.stepSummary: If the stones count against the whole ones anyway, recognizing them seems to give him nothing.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, what does it help him?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges אביי's reading. It sets up the next step, which explains the gain.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Under אביי, the recognizer ends up with the same number of whole stones he would have gotten anyway. So why does the משנה even mention that he recognized them?

phrases.english: If so,
what does it help him?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges אביי's reading from step 20
steps.kashyaTarget: אביי's reading that the stones count against the whole stones
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If he gets the same number of whole stones either way, recognizing his stones seems to make no difference

steps.title: He gets bigger or better-made bricks
steps.stepSummary: His own bricks may be bigger, from a wide mold, or made of better-processed clay.
steps.simpleTranslation: It helps in a case of a wide brick mold. Or also, clay that was processed well.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that recognizing his own stones helps him get better stones, even if the number stays the same.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His bricks may be larger because they came from a wider mold, or stronger because the clay was prepared better. So he gains in quality, not in quantity.
steps.whatToRemember: According to אביי, recognizing your stones does not give you more whole stones. It gives you your own stones, which may be bigger or better made.

phrases.english: For a wide brick mold.
phrases.notes: A wider mold makes bigger bricks, so getting his own bricks means getting larger ones.

phrases.english: Or also, clay that was processed well.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 21
steps.terutzResolutionType: Points to a gain in quality, not quantity
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Recognizing his stones gives him nothing under אביי
steps.terutzMaskana: He gains bigger bricks from a wide mold, or bricks of better-processed clay

steps.title: Upstairs resident may move downstairs
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that if the upper story's floor breaks and the owner won't fix it, the upstairs resident lives downstairs until it is fixed.
steps.simpleTranslation: MISHNA: A house and an upper story. If the upper story broke through, and the owner of the house does not want to repair it, the resident of the upper story goes down and lives below until the owner fixes the upper story for him.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It rules that an upstairs resident whose floor broke may move into the downstairs part of the house until the owner repairs it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The owner owes this person a place to live. If he refuses to fix the upper story, he cannot leave the resident without a home, so the resident may use the lower floor in the meantime. The case pictures one owner of the whole building, with the upper story given to someone else to live in.

keyTerms.meaning: Short for מתניתין, meaning 'our משנה'. It marks the start of a new משנה.
An upper story or upstairs apartment.
It broke through or caved in. Here it refers to the floor of the upper story.
The person living in the upper story.

steps.confusionAlert: In this first case the בעל העלייה is the person living upstairs, not a separate owner. The building belongs to the בעל הבית, which is why he must fix it. The case with two separate owners comes in רבי יוסי's line.

phrases.english: MISHNA: A house and an upper story.
If the upper story broke through,
and the owner of the house does not want to repair it,

phrases.aramaic: הֲרֵי בַּעַל הָעֲלִיָּיה יוֹרֵד וְדָר לְמַטָּה,
phrases.english: then the resident of the upper story goes down and lives below,
until he repairs the upper story for him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה after the discussion of the fallen stones ended.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If the owner won't fix a broken upper story, the resident may live downstairs until it is repaired.

steps.title: How two owners split the ceiling repair
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי says the lower owner supplies the ceiling and the upper owner supplies the plaster.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוסי says: The lower one provides the ceiling, and the upper one provides the plaster.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוסי adds a rule for a building owned by two people, one downstairs and one upstairs. He divides who pays for which part of the broken ceiling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ceiling beams serve as the roof of the lower owner's home, so he provides them. The plaster forms the floor that the upper owner walks on, so he provides it.

keyTerms.meaning: The lower one, meaning the owner of the downstairs.
The upper one, meaning the owner of the upstairs.
The ceiling, made of beams or boards.
The layer of plaster spread on top of the ceiling, which makes the upstairs floor.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei says:
The lower one provides the ceiling,
and the upper one provides the plaster.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second ruling to the same משנה, for a building with two owners.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The lower owner provides the ceiling beams, and the upper owner provides the plaster.

steps.title: How big must the break be?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how large the break in the floor must be for the משנה's rule to apply.
steps.simpleTranslation: GEMARA: It broke through — by how much?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins and asks a clarifying question about the משנה's word 'broke'. This sets up the next step, where two אמוראים will answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה lets the resident move downstairs, but it never says how much damage that takes. A small crack surely isn't enough, so the גמרא wants the size that makes the upstairs no longer livable.

keyTerms.meaning: Short for גמרא. It marks where the גמרא's discussion of the משנה begins.

phrases.english: GEMARA: It broke through — by how much?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the גמרא's discussion of the משנה in step 23.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What size of break counts as 'broken' for the resident to be allowed to move downstairs.

steps.title: Most of the floor, or four טפחים
steps.stepSummary: רב says most of the floor must break. שמואל says a break of four טפחים is enough.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב says: Most of it. And שמואל says: Four.
steps.whatsHappening: Two אמוראים answer the question. רב needs a larger break than שמואל does.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב requires most of the floor to be broken before the resident may move. שמואל sets a much smaller amount, a hole of four טפחים. So by שמואל, even a fairly small hole lets the resident go downstairs.

keyTerms.meaning: In most of it, meaning the majority of the floor.
By four, meaning a hole of four טפחים.

phrases.english: Rav says: Most of it,
and Shmuel says: Four.
phrases.notes: Four means four טפחים, which are handbreadths.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב אָמַר: בְּרוּבָּהּ, וּשְׁמוּאֵל אָמַר: בְּאַרְבָּעָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 25.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רב: most of the floor. שמואל: a break of four טפחים.

steps.title: רב's reason: a person can live split
steps.stepSummary: רב holds that four טפחים is not enough, because a person can live partly downstairs and partly upstairs.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב says: Most of it, but four — no, because a person does live half below and half above.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא repeats רב's view in order to explain his reasoning. A small hole doesn't count, since the resident can stay upstairs and use the lower floor for the rest.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By רב, a four-טפח hole doesn't make the upstairs unlivable. The resident can keep living upstairs and place whatever would have gone in the broken spot downstairs. Only when most of the floor is gone must he be allowed to move down.

keyTerms.meaning: Half below and half above: living partly downstairs and partly upstairs.

phrases.english: Rav says: Most of it,
but four — no,
because a person does live half below
and half above.
phrases.notes: He means the resident can stay upstairs and use the downstairs for the part he lost.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָדָם דָּר חֶצְיוֹ לְמַטָּה וְחֶצְיוֹ לְמַעְלָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the reasoning behind רב's answer in step 26.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A four-טפח hole is not enough, since a person can live split between two floors.

steps.title: שמואל's reason: no one lives split
steps.stepSummary: שמואל holds that four טפחים is enough, because a person cannot be expected to live partly downstairs and partly upstairs.
steps.simpleTranslation: And שמואל says: Four, because a person does not live half below and half above.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives שמואל's reasoning, which is the exact opposite of רב's. People do not live split between two floors, so even a four-טפח hole lets the resident move down.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The whole מחלוקת comes down to one question: is it a normal way to live, to be partly on one floor and partly on another? רב says yes, so a small hole is bearable. שמואל says no, so a small hole already means the upper story is not a proper home.

keyTerms.meaning: A person does not live (that way).

steps.whatToRemember: רב: only a break in most of the floor counts, because a person can live split between floors. שמואל: four טפחים is enough, because a person cannot live split between floors.

phrases.english: And Shmuel says: Four,
because a person does not live half below
and half above.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֵין אָדָם דָּר חֶצְיוֹ לְמַטָּה וְחֶצְיוֹ לְמַעְלָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives שמואל's reasoning, which mirrors and opposes רב's reasoning in step 27.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A four-טפח hole is enough, since a person does not live split between two floors.

steps.title: What case could the rule possibly be talking about?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא tests both possible ways the rental could have been worded, and neither one fits the rule.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the case? If the owner said 'this upper story,' then once it breaks, it's gone, and the renter has lost out. But if he said just 'an upper story' without naming one, the owner should rent him a different upper story somewhere else.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks how the rental was worded, since the rule lets the renter move downstairs. It shows that both obvious options cause a problem.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a specific upper story was rented, the renter's rights end when it breaks, so he should have no claim on the house below. If an unnamed upper story was rented, the owner should simply supply another upper story. Either way, 'move downstairs' does not seem to be the right result.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case? What are the circumstances?
An upper story, an apartment on top of a house
It is gone, it no longer exists

steps.confusionAlert: This is not just a request for information. The גמרא is showing that both possible cases fail, so it is really a challenge.

phrases.english: What are the circumstances?
If he said "this upper story"
phrases.notes: The owner pointed to one specific upper story when he rented it out.

phrases.english: it is gone!
Rather, where he said to him "an upper story" without specifying
then let him rent him a different one.

steps.triggerLanguage: הֵיכִי דָמֵי? אִי דְּאָמַר עֲלִיָּיה זוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns from the size of the break to the wording of the rental that would justify moving downstairs.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule that a renter whose upper story broke may live in the house below
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A specific rental ends when the upper story is destroyed. An unspecified rental calls for a replacement upper story. Neither leads to moving downstairs.

steps.title: רבא: The owner said 'go up with it and down with it'
steps.stepSummary: רבא suggests that the owner said outright that the renter goes wherever the upper story goes.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: The rule is needed for a case where the owner told him, 'This upper story that I am renting you: when it is up, live up there with it, and when it comes down, come down with it.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבא answers the challenge. He says the owner made an explicit condition that the renter moves down if the upper story falls.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This explains why the renter gets the house below: the owner promised it out loud. It gets around the problem that a specific rental would otherwise simply end.

keyTerms.meaning: It is needed only for... (this specific case)

phrases.english: Rava said: It is needed only

phrases.aramaic: דַּאֲמַר לֵיהּ: עֲלִיָּיה זוֹ שֶׁאֲנִי מַשְׂכִּיר לָךְ,
phrases.english: where he said to him: This upper story that I am renting to you,
when it is up, go up with it,
phrases.notes: He means: as long as the upper story stands and can be lived in, live up there.

phrases.english: and when it comes down, come down with it.
phrases.notes: The letter in square brackets is added in the corrected wording.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge by suggesting a third kind of wording.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The rental had to be either a specific upper story or an unnamed one, and both fail.
steps.terutzMaskana: The owner explicitly promised that the renter would move down with the upper story.

steps.title: Then why would the rule need to be taught?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that if the owner said this outright, the rule is obvious.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, what is the point of saying it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on רבא. If the owner clearly promised the downstairs, of course the renter moves down, so there is nothing new to teach.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A legal teaching is supposed to tell us something we would not have known. An explicit condition just enforces itself, so רבא's case makes the rule pointless.

keyTerms.meaning: What is there to say? Why is this needed? (it's obvious)

phrases.english: If so, what is the point of saying it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects רבא's answer because it makes the rule obvious.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's case of an explicit condition
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the condition was stated, the result is plain. The rule would be teaching nothing new.

steps.title: רב אשי: 'This upper story on top of this house'
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי says the owner described the upper story as being on top of a particular house, and that ties the house to it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רב אשי said: The case is where the owner said, 'I am renting you this upper story, which is on top of this house.' By saying that, he made the house bound to the upper story.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי gives a new answer. The owner did not promise the downstairs outright, but he named the house underneath, and that quietly binds the house to the rental.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This wording sits in the middle. It is more than a plain specific rental, which would just end when the upper story breaks. It is less than an explicit promise, which would make the rule obvious. Because the house was mentioned, it serves as backing for the upper story, so the renter may move down. That is something new to teach.

keyTerms.meaning: He made it bound, put a lien on it

steps.whatToRemember: The final answer is that saying 'this upper story on top of this house' ties the house below to the rental. If the upper story breaks, the renter may live in the house.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that how a deal is worded, even without an explicit condition, can create a binding right to a backup property.

phrases.english: Rather, Rav Ashi said:
where he said to him: "This upper story

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁעַל גַּבֵּי בַּיִת זֶה אֲנִי מַשְׂכִּיר לָךְ״,
phrases.english: which is on top of this house I am renting to you,"
for he has made the house bound to the upper story.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces רבא's rejected answer with a wording that avoids both problems.
steps.terutzResolutionType: New case definition: wording that implies a lien
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The only way to get the downstairs seemed to be an explicit condition, which would make the rule obvious.
steps.terutzMaskana: Naming the house underneath creates a lien without saying so outright. This is not obvious, so it is worth teaching.

steps.title: Support: the vine sold on top of a peach tree
steps.stepSummary: A ruling by רבי חייא, about a vine sold 'on top of this peach tree,' matches רב אשי's idea.
steps.simpleTranslation: This fits what רבין בר רב אדא said in the name of רבי יצחק: Someone told his friend, 'I am selling you the vine that is on top of this peach tree,' and then the peach tree was uprooted. The case came before רבי חייא, and he said: You must set up a peach tree for him to hold the vine for as long as the vine lives.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a similar case to back up רב אשי. Describing the vine as sitting 'on top of this tree' made the seller responsible for keeping up its support.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Just like the house under the upper story, the peach tree was named as the support for the item sold. So when the support is gone, the seller must replace it. This shows that mentioning the support in the deal binds the seller to it.

keyTerms.meaning: A grapevine trained to climb on a tree

phrases.aramaic: וְכִי הָא דְּאָמַר רָבִין בַּר רַב אַדָּא
phrases.english: And this is like what Ravin bar Rav Adda said
that Rabbi Yitzchak said:
There was an incident with someone who said to his friend

phrases.aramaic: ״דָּלִית שֶׁעַל גַּבֵּי פַּרְסֵק זֶה אֲנִי מוֹכֵר לָךְ״,
phrases.english: "I am selling you the vine that is on top of this peach tree,"
and the peach tree was uprooted.

phrases.aramaic: וּבָא מַעֲשֶׂה לִפְנֵי רַבִּי חִיָּיא, וְאָמַר:
phrases.english: And the case came before Rabbi Chiyya, and he said:
You must set up a peach tree for him
phrases.notes: The new tree is there to hold up the vine, the way the old one did.

phrases.english: for as long as the vine is alive.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי הָא דְּאָמַר רָבִין בַּר רַב אַדָּא אָמַר רַבִּי יִצְחָק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a parallel ruling that supports רב אשי's reasoning.
steps.raayaObject: רב אשי's principle that naming the support in a deal binds it to the item
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי חייא's ruling, reported by רבי יצחק, in the case of the vine on the peach tree

steps.title: רבי אבא בר ממל introduces a new question
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא opens a new section by announcing that רבי אבא בר ממל asked a question. The question itself follows right after.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבא בר ממל asked a question:
steps.whatsHappening: This is a setup line. The גמרא is telling us that רבי אבא בר ממל is about to ask an open question, and the actual question comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word בעי signals a real question that a scholar was unsure about, not a challenge against someone else's view. The previous discussion about the rental wording is finished, and a fresh topic is starting. At this point nothing has been asked yet. Keep reading to the next line to see what the question is.

keyTerms.meaning: He asked, or he raised a question he was unsure about
An open question that a scholar raises because he does not yet know the answer
An אמורא from ארץ ישראל who raises the question here

steps.confusionAlert: Don't read בעי as an attack or a קשיא. It introduces an honest question where the asker does not know the answer. It is not an objection to an earlier statement.

phrases.english: Rabbi Abba bar Memel raised a dilemma:

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new section after the discussion of the rental wording ended with the proof from רבי חייא in step 33.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: This line only introduces the question. The question itself comes on the next amud.
